contents.description: Rooftop solar panels are designed differently, operating without an engine, fuel, or moving parts. They generate power by light knocking electrons loose from treated silicon, costing approximately ₹60,000 per kilowatt. A panel converts sunlight directly into electricity, powering homes and feeding surplus to the grid, lasting around 25 years with only electrons moving internally. The panel structure includes a durable glass face, silicon cells, a metal frame, and is tilted to maximize sun exposure. Internally, it comprises a tough glass layer, silicon cells with silver current lines, a back sheet, and a junction box. The core technology, a silicon wafer made from treated sand, uses silver fingers to collect current and a busbar to carry it. When light strikes the silicon, it frees an electron, which an electric field then pushes, creating a flow of electrons that constitutes electricity. The panel, however, is only part of the system; an inverter converts the direct current (DC) it produces into alternating current (AC) for household use and the grid. This allows homes to feed spare power to the grid during the day and draw credit back at night, preventing off-grid operation. Financially, a 1 kW rooftop setup costs about ₹60,000, with subsidies like PM Surya Ghar reducing the initial outlay. Systems typically achieve payback in four to five years through reduced bills, providing free power for an additional two decades, effectively pre-purchasing decades of electricity. The system's key benefits are that nothing moves and nothing burns, prompting consideration for installation.
contents.caption: A rooftop solar panel has no engine, no fuel and no moving parts. When sunlight strikes the silicon it knocks electrons loose, and a built-in electric field at the junction sweeps them into a wire as direct current. An inverter turns that into home AC, and net metering banks your daytime surplus for the night. Here is the physics that pays for itself, from about 60,000 rupees a kW.
